body_markdown:
Well, Elon, that was mighty impressive, indeed.


By this point, calling Tesla (or its figurehead) a divisive topic would probably be an understatement. Still, following last week’s presentation, I have to hand it to Elon & Co: They really know how to put on a show.


Musk has always been adamant that, despite shipping well over a million cars a year, Tesla isn’t so much a car company as a technology one. It’s a story that investors worldwide still largely believe, as the company’s staggering $1.4 trillion market cap utterly dwarfs that of any other automaker on the planet. But if we ever needed more proof that Tesla really doesn’t operate like a car company, last week’s presentation of the new Roadster was it.


Tesla


Does our messy, troubled world need[a car that can fly](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22rvpUecLts&list=PLHKCmmH-x9mK5F-KoK4jm0_7KnT5uyVZp&index=1) ? Or one that comes with thrusters on the back to accelerate faster? Of course not. But boy, I’d be a liar if I said that seeing the new Roadster behave like a Hot Wheels in a child’s hand didn’t brighten my day way more than it probably should. Yes, deliveries won’t happen until 2028, if at all, and half the things the Roadster does will no doubt make the heads of EU bureaucrats in Brussels explode. For now, none of that matters, though. Because, as quaint as that may sound, it’s refreshing to see a car once again be a vision of what’s possible. In a world where people often seek comfort in the past, and future expectations seem loaded with fear and disillusionment, it’s invigorating to be reminded that we, as a species, can do pretty darn cool things when we want to.


But setting aside its technology and capabilities for a moment, how does the new Roadster stack up as a[pure design statement](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/) ? Where does it stand in today’s car design landscape, and what does it say about the future of the automobile?


Tesla


Well, I think the best way to answer such heavy questions is to break down the Roadster’s design into its basic elements, starting, of course, from its proportions.


In this regard, the new Tesla Roadster adheres strictly to the classic supercar formula as it was established by Marcello Gandini well over half a century ago. It’s as pure a wedge shape as it gets, its profile one unbroken line from the low, sloping nose to the tall, sharply cut tail. The cabin is pushed far forward, as we’ve gotten so used to seeing on Lamborghinis, only this time the decision allowed the designers to pack in a pressurized nitrogen tank rather than a V-12 engine.


Tesla


Tesla


Tesla


But the Lamborghini analogies don’t stop there; even the way the Roadster’s volume is sculpted gives off a similar vibe. Large, unbroken surfaces with sharp creases and even sharper radii make the Countach immediately spring to mind, while the front-end treatment evokes more modern Lambos like the Murciélago or the Huracán. Minimalist to the point of starkness, the razor-sharp Roadster fits right in the direction we’ve seen both Jaguar and Audi take with their latest concept cars, but, at least from the pictures, the Tesla appears to lack that degree of refinement in the modeling of the surfaces that’s made the Audi Nuvolari such a hit with critics and the public alike.


Tesla


Tesla


In particular, I think the surfacing on the Roadster’s flanks and rear end could have been better judged to give off a more pleasing sense of robustness, like a piece hewn from a solid block. As is, the Roadster’s panels look somewhat fragile, even though I’m sure they actually aren’t: It’s simply a visual thing. Like the Robotaxi that disappointed me so much two years ago, the Roadster’s surfacing makes the whole design feel a tad underbaked to my eye, as if it could have benefited from a bit more time and care in the clay room.


Lamborghini Countach LP 500


Lamborghini


It’s funny to see just how similar the future looks to how Gandini envisioned it back in 1971, when he was designing the original Countach prototype. In fact, it reminds me of what I like to say to design students at the end of one of my favorite classes, where I go through the golden era of the Italian *“Carrozzeria.”* The idea is that the work of people like Gandini, like that of Renaissance artists such as Michelangelo, continues to inspire new creations because it forms part of our shared cultural heritage. So, while the time when houses like Bertone could act as global tastemakers may be long gone, their influence, from what I can see, is still far from over.


Coming back to the Roadster, the last ingredients to analyze are the graphics and details, which I find all coherent with the clean, minimalist techno vibe that characterizes the whole project. The Roadster’s thin, full-width daytime running lights are a refreshingly simple, neat touch, but the real surprise is the main headlights. Not only are they the slimmest, most compact units we’ve seen so far on any vehicle, but they are hidden under flaps, in a sort of “reverse-pop-up” solution that’s a charming reinterpretation of the retractable headlights of old and completes the “transformer” vibe of a vehicle that already has plenty of elements that move.


Tesla


Tesla


Tesla


The whole diffuser/fan area at the rear is also quite neatly resolved. In fact, it seems much less messy and cumbersome than on most modern supercars and, as usual, is finished in a darker shade to lighten the rear end visually. It’s detached from an upper section that seems to “float” above it and, again, evokes, at least to my eye, the Countach and its Diablo successor.


As of now, it remains to be seen whether this latest iteration of the Roadster will deliver, or whether it is a mere flash of showmanship. From a pure styling standpoint, it’s somewhat safe and derivative, if cleanly penned. But it sure has already made history, and if it actually ends up hitting the road, I have little doubt that the sheer wow factor of its unique technology and features will make it the first genuinely desirable, and thus successful, electric supercar.

*Matteo Licata received his degree in Transportation Design from Turin’s IED (Istituto Europeo di Design) in 2006. He worked as an automobile designer for about a decade, including a stint in the then-Fiat Group’s Turin design studio, during which his proposal for the interior of the 2010–20 Alfa Romeo Giulietta was selected for production. He next joined Changan’s European design studio in Turin and then EDAG in Barcelona, Spain. Licata currently teaches automobile design history to the Transportation Design bachelor students of IAAD (Istituto di Arte Applicata e Design) in Turin.*
